title: Status: Know It
greet: Hey, it’s Lensy. 🩺 Testing is self-care, not shame. Build your prevention stack, know treatment works, and stand for dignity: zero stigma.

badge.title: Status: Know It! 🩺
badge.blurb: You know testing is power not shame, can build a prevention stack and talk to a partner, know treatment works (U=U), and stand for dignity with zero stigma. 💛

helpLine: Free HIV/STI testing: find a NACO ICTC centre or ask a doctor, who will explain what stays private. If anyone pressures or exploits you, call Childline 1098.
reassure: Testing is power, not shame: an STI or HIV is a health matter, never a verdict; with treatment people live full lives (U=U). If pressured, call Childline 1098.

scenarios.hook: "Getting tested means you did something wrong."

myth.un: Getting tested means you did something wrong.
myth.re: Testing is routine, responsible self-care, like any other health check.
myth.why: Knowing your status is how you look after yourself and others.

scenarios.relearn: Testing is smart self-care, not an admission of guilt.

scenarios.hook: "Only certain kinds of people need to get tested."

myth.un: Only certain kinds of people need testing.
myth.re: Testing is about behaviour, not identity; anyone sexually active can benefit.
myth.why: Linking it to 'types of people' is stigma, not science.

scenarios.relearn: Testing is about behaviour, not identity; it's for anyone active.

scenarios.hook: "You can tell if someone has an STI just by looking."

myth.un: You can tell someone's status by looking at them.
myth.re: Many STIs have no visible signs; only testing tells you.
myth.why: Looks reveal nothing; a test reveals the facts.

scenarios.relearn: You can't tell status by looking; only a test tells you.

scenarios.hook: "Home or self-tests aren't reliable."

myth.un: Self-tests aren't reliable.
myth.re: Self-tests are reliable when used correctly and read after the window period.
myth.why: They're a valid, private way to know your status.

scenarios.relearn: Self-tests are reliable when used right and read after the window period.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a reason testing is smart, or a stigma myth?

items.text: It lets you act on the facts
It puts you in charge of your health

scenarios.relearn: Acting, protecting and taking charge are smart; 'dirty', 'those people' and 'branded' are stigma.

scenarios.relearn: Windows, free confidential care and valid self-tests are true; 'one forever', symptom-only and 'tell by looking' are myths.

scenarios.affirm: A result is data to act on, never a judgement on who you are.

myth.re: PrEP is a smart, judgment-free HIV-prevention tool for anyone who could benefit.
myth.why: Prevention is responsible, not a character flaw.

scenarios.relearn: PrEP is a smart prevention tool, no judgment attached.

myth.re: PrEP helps prevent HIV but not other STIs; condoms still add protection.
myth.why: Different tools cover different risks.

scenarios.relearn: PrEP prevents HIV, not other STIs; condoms still matter.

scenarios.hook: Sort: part of a complete stack, or leaves a gap?
scenarios.relearn: Combining tools and testing closes gaps; assuming or skipping leaves them.

scenarios.affirm: You assemble it, you own it, that's prevention as power.

scenarios.affirm: Delaying is the most certain option and entirely respected, alongside every tool.
scenarios.relearn: Delaying remains fully respected and the most certain option.

items.text: Condoms reduce both STI and pregnancy risk
You can't tell status by looking

scenarios.relearn: Condoms, PrEP and 'can't tell by looking' are facts; 'pointless' and 'one is enough' are myths.

myth.un: Talking about testing and protection ruins the moment.
myth.re: A caring partner welcomes it; looking after each other is part of intimacy.
myth.why: The talk is care, not a mood-killer.

scenarios.relearn: Talking about protection is care; a good partner welcomes it.

scenarios.hook: "Asking a partner to test means you don't trust them."

myth.re: It's mutual care and normal health practice, not an accusation.
myth.why: Status isn't about trust; it's about facts neither of you can see.

scenarios.relearn: Asking to test is mutual care, not distrust.

scenarios.affirm: Open health talk is one of the most caring things partners do.
scenarios.relearn: Talking about sexual health is an act of care.

scenarios.hook: "If you really cared you wouldn't ask me to test."

myth.re: Asking is exactly what caring looks like; it protects you both.
myth.why: Guilt-flipping the ask is a pressure tactic.

scenarios.relearn: Asking to test is caring; guilt-flipping it is a pressure tactic.

options.consequence: You start from shared knowledge and care.

options.text: Assume you're both fine without checking
options.consequence: Testing together and agreeing protection beats assuming.

scenarios.debrief: Shared testing and an agreed plan is the responsible, caring baseline.
scenarios.relearn: Test together and agree on protection, as equals.

scenarios.hook: "An HIV diagnosis is a death sentence."

myth.un: An HIV diagnosis is a death sentence.
myth.re: With treatment HIV is a manageable long-term condition and people live full, healthy lives.
myth.why: Modern treatment changed the picture completely.

scenarios.relearn: HIV is manageable with treatment; people live full, healthy lives.

scenarios.hook: "Someone on HIV treatment can still easily pass it on."

myth.un: Someone on treatment can still easily pass HIV on.
myth.re: Undetectable = untransmittable (U=U): effective treatment means it can't be sexually transmitted.
myth.why: Studies found zero transmissions from an undetectable partner.

scenarios.relearn: U=U: on effective treatment, HIV can't be sexually passed on.

scenarios.hook: "STIs are permanent and there's nothing you can do."

myth.un: STIs are permanent and untreatable.
myth.re: Most are treatable and several (chlamydia, gonorrhoea, syphilis, trichomoniasis) are curable.
myth.why: A diagnosis is something to act on, not endure forever.

scenarios.relearn: Most STIs are treatable; several are fully curable.

scenarios.hook: "There's no point testing, because nothing can be done anyway."

myth.un: There's no point testing; nothing can be done.
myth.re: Testing leads to treatment that works; the sooner you know, the better the outcome.
myth.why: Early action is exactly what makes treatment effective.

scenarios.relearn: Testing leads to treatment that works; knowing early helps most.

scenarios.hook: Sort: curable, or managed long-term?
scenarios.relearn: Chlamydia, gonorrhoea, syphilis and trichomoniasis are curable; HIV and herpes are managed.

scenarios.hook: Sort: true about treatment, or a fear myth?

"You'll always be too sick to work"

scenarios.relearn: Undetectable, treatable STIs and free care are true; the doom myths are false.

scenarios.relearn: U=U, undetectable, curable, managed and ART are the hopeful facts of treatment.

scenarios.affirm: When you know treatment works, knowing your status feels safe, not scary.
scenarios.relearn: Knowing treatment works makes testing feel safe, not frightening.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: a diagnosis is information to act on, not a verdict on your character. Agree?
scenarios.affirm: A result says nothing about your worth, it's simply a cue to act.
scenarios.relearn: A diagnosis is a cue to act, never a verdict on your character.

options.text: Leave them to it
options.consequence: A few facts, power, treatment, no shame, could help them start; share them.

scenarios.debrief: Passing on 'power, treatment, dignity' can free a friend to act.
scenarios.relearn: Share 'testing is power, treatment works, no shame' to help a friend act.

scenarios.hook: "You can tell who has an STI by how they look or live."

myth.un: You can tell who has an STI by how they look or live.
myth.re: You can't tell from looks or lifestyle; only a test tells, and a result says nothing about worth.
myth.why: Linking infection to 'type of person' is stigma, not fact.

scenarios.relearn: You can't tell by looking; a result is never a verdict on a person.

scenarios.hook: "People living with HIV shouldn't share utensils or sit close."

myth.un: People living with HIV shouldn't share utensils or sit close.
myth.re: HIV doesn't spread by sharing food, hugging or sitting together; exclusion is stigma, not safety.
myth.why: Everyday contact carries no risk; shunning only causes harm.

scenarios.relearn: Sharing food, hugs and seats are safe; exclusion is stigma, not protection.

scenarios.hook: "If you get an STI, you should keep quiet and just live with the shame."

myth.un: If you get an STI, you should keep quiet and just live with the shame.
myth.re: There's nothing to be ashamed of; it's a health matter you can test for and treat with dignity.
myth.why: Shame keeps people from care; an infection is not a character flaw.

scenarios.relearn: An STI is a health matter, not a shame to carry; you deserve care.

scenarios.hook: "Refusing to hire or seat someone because of their status is just being careful."

myth.un: Refusing to hire or seat someone because of their status is just being careful.
myth.re: Status is no reason to exclude anyone; that's discrimination, and the person deserves equal treatment.
myth.why: There's no everyday risk, so exclusion is only stigma dressed up as caution.

scenarios.relearn: Excluding someone over status isn't caution; it's discrimination.

scenarios.hook: "A married person can't have an STI, so testing would insult them."

myth.un: A married person can't have an STI, so testing would insult them.
myth.re: Marriage doesn't make anyone immune; testing is routine self-care, not an insult to anyone.
myth.why: Status is about health, not respectability or relationship status.

scenarios.relearn: Marriage isn't immunity; testing is care, not an insult.

scenarios.hook: "Naming someone's status in the family WhatsApp is just keeping everyone informed."

myth.un: Naming someone's status in the family WhatsApp is just keeping everyone informed.
myth.re: Their status is private; sharing it without consent isn't 'informing', it's breaking trust.
myth.why: Confidentiality is part of dignity; it's theirs to share, not yours.

scenarios.relearn: Posting someone's status isn't informing; it breaks their privacy.

scenarios.hook: "People with HIV are dangerous and should be kept away from kids."

myth.un: People with HIV are dangerous and should be kept away from kids.
myth.re: They're parents, teachers and neighbours like anyone; HIV isn't spread by everyday care or contact.
myth.why: Fear-based exclusion harms families and is not based in fact.

scenarios.relearn: People with HIV care for kids safely; exclusion is fear, not fact.

scenarios.hook: "Once people know your status, your life is basically over."

myth.un: Once people know your status, your life is basically over.
myth.re: Status doesn't end a life or define worth; on treatment people study, work and love fully.
myth.why: It's the stigma, not the virus, that does this damage, and stigma can be refused.

scenarios.relearn: Status doesn't end your life or your worth; treatment lets you thrive.

scenarios.hook: "It's funny to use 'AIDS' as an insult."

myth.un: It's funny to use 'AIDS' as an insult.
myth.re: Using a health condition as a slur mocks real people and spreads stigma; it isn't a joke.
myth.why: Slurs make people hide and avoid testing, which causes real harm.

scenarios.relearn: Using a condition as an insult isn't a joke; it harms real people.

scenarios.hook: "A counsellor can tell your parents your result if they ask."

myth.un: A counsellor can tell your parents your result if they ask.
myth.re: Your result is confidential; an ICTC counsellor protects your privacy, it's not shared on demand.
myth.why: Confidentiality is built into the service so people feel safe to test.

scenarios.relearn: Your result is confidential; the service protects your privacy.

scenarios.hook: "Being scared of catching it from a classmate is reasonable."

myth.un: Being scared of catching it from a classmate is reasonable.
myth.re: You won't catch HIV from sitting, sharing notes or eating together; the fear comes from myths, not risk.
myth.why: Knowing the real routes replaces fear with calm and respect.

scenarios.relearn: Everyday classroom contact carries no HIV risk; fear comes from myths.

scenarios.hook: "If a partner discloses their status, the kind thing is to pity them."

myth.un: If a partner discloses their status, the kind thing is to pity them.
myth.re: They want respect, not pity; meet honesty with warmth and treat them as the same equal person.
myth.why: Pity looks down on someone; dignity stands beside them.

scenarios.relearn: Meet a disclosure with respect, not pity; they're the same person.

scenarios.hook: "People who get an STI were careless and brought it on themselves."

myth.un: People who get an STI were careless and brought it on themselves.
myth.re: Infections happen for many reasons and aren't a measure of character; everyone deserves care.
myth.why: Blame is stigma; it stops people seeking the help that works.

scenarios.relearn: An infection isn't a character verdict; blame just blocks care.

scenarios.hook: "You should dump a friend who tells you they're living with HIV."

myth.un: You should dump a friend who tells you they're living with HIV.
myth.re: They trusted you with something private; staying a steady, normal friend is exactly what dignity looks like.
myth.why: A disclosure is a sign of trust, not a reason to walk away.

scenarios.relearn: A friend's disclosure is trust; stay the same steady friend.

scenarios.hook: "Self-blame after a diagnosis just means you're being responsible."

myth.un: Self-blame after a diagnosis just means you're being responsible.
myth.re: You can be responsible without shame; treat yourself with the same dignity you'd give a friend.
myth.why: Self-stigma harms you and can delay the care that helps.

scenarios.relearn: Being responsible doesn't need self-blame; give yourself dignity too.

scenarios.hook: "The red ribbon is about feeling sorry for sick people."

myth.un: The red ribbon is about feeling sorry for sick people.
myth.re: The red ribbon stands for solidarity and support, standing with people, not pitying them.
myth.why: Solidarity respects people as equals; pity sets them apart.

scenarios.relearn: The red ribbon means solidarity and support, not pity.

scenarios.hook: "It's fine to ask a new colleague their status before working with them."

myth.un: It's fine to ask a new colleague their status before working with them.
myth.re: Their status is private and not your business; working together carries no everyday risk.
myth.why: Demanding private health info is intrusive and based on myth.

scenarios.relearn: A colleague's status is private and not needed to work together.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: dignity means the same warm hello whether or not you know someone's status. Sit with that?
scenarios.affirm: A person's worth doesn't shift with a test result, your respect doesn't have to either.
scenarios.relearn: Someone's worth, and your respect, don't change with a result.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: if a friend ever told you their status, how would you want to show up for them?
scenarios.affirm: Any of these honours their trust, showing up steady and warm is what they'll remember.
scenarios.relearn: Honour a disclosure by listening, staying steady and offering support.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: notice the urge to gossip when you hear who got tested, what would you rather do?
scenarios.affirm: Choosing not to pass it on protects someone's privacy, that quiet choice is real dignity.
scenarios.relearn: Protecting someone's privacy is a quiet, real act of dignity.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: dignity includes how you'd talk to yourself after a hard result. What tone would you choose?
scenarios.affirm: You deserve the same kindness you'd give anyone, your worth is whole, result or not.
scenarios.relearn: Speak to yourself with the kindness you'd give a friend; your worth is whole.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: a classroom where no one fears judgement is one where people actually go test. Want that?
scenarios.affirm: Every bit of judgement you drop makes it safer for someone near you to look after their health.
scenarios.relearn: Less judgement around you makes it safer for people to test.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: when you hear 'they must have done something', what's the kinder, truer thought?
scenarios.affirm: Dropping the blame story sees the human first, that's where dignity starts.
scenarios.relearn: Replace the blame story with 'anyone can be affected'.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: picture someone disclosing to you on a long bus ride home. What would you want them to feel?
scenarios.affirm: Whatever words you'd use, the feeling you give, safe and unjudged, is the heart of dignity.
scenarios.relearn: Aim to leave someone feeling safe and unjudged after they disclose.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: stigma is a habit you can unlearn, like flinching. Ready to notice yours?
scenarios.affirm: Noticing the reflex is step one, every time you choose dignity instead, the habit weakens.
scenarios.relearn: Stigma is a reflex you can notice and unlearn, one choice at a time.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: imagine your name attached to a kind, fact-based comment under a stigma post. Feel okay?
scenarios.affirm: A calm, factual voice in a noisy thread can quietly change how a whole room thinks.
scenarios.relearn: A calm, factual reply to stigma can shift a whole conversation.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: dignity for yourself means you can still dream big after a diagnosis. Believe that?
scenarios.affirm: Your studies, work and love life are still yours, a result manages, it doesn't cancel.
scenarios.relearn: A diagnosis is managed, not the end of your plans or dreams.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: who in your life would you want to feel safe enough to tell you anything about their health?
scenarios.affirm: Being that safe person is something you build, with every judgement-free reaction.
scenarios.relearn: You become a 'safe person' through judgement-free reactions.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: hostel rumour says someone went to a clinic. What's the dignified move with that rumour?
scenarios.affirm: Letting a rumour die with you is a small, powerful act of respect for someone you may not even know.
scenarios.relearn: Let a health rumour stop with you; that's respect in action.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: 'I know my status, and I still deserve dignity.' Can you say that for yourself?
scenarios.affirm: That sentence is yours to keep, your dignity was never up for the test in the first place.
scenarios.relearn: Your dignity isn't on the line at any test; it's always yours.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: a relative jokes about a neighbour's 'illness'. What sits right for you to do?
scenarios.affirm: You don't owe a laugh to a cruel joke, even silence can refuse to feed stigma.
scenarios.relearn: You can refuse stigma simply by not laughing along.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: what would a school feel like where 'get tested' was as normal as 'get your eyes checked'?
scenarios.affirm: That's the world dignity builds, where caring for your health needs no courage at all.
scenarios.relearn: Dignity makes testing as ordinary as any other health check.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: someone you admire turns out to be living with HIV. Does it change your admiration?
scenarios.affirm: Who they are didn't change with a result, and noticing that is dignity working in you.
scenarios.relearn: A status doesn't change who someone is or what they've done.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: dignity is a choice you own, no one assigns it. How do you want to spend that choice?
scenarios.affirm: Spent on respect, your choice ripples, the way you treat one person teaches everyone watching.
scenarios.relearn: Treating people with dignity is a choice you own and others learn from.

scenarios.hook: Sort: dignity for yourself, or self-stigma?
scenarios.relearn: Treatment, worth and dreams are self-dignity; 'dirty', 'deserve' and 'hide' are self-stigma.

scenarios.hook: Sort: solidarity, or pity?

Wearing the red ribbon to stand with people

scenarios.relearn: Standing with people as equals is solidarity; 'poor thing' and looking down are pity.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a calm fact about HIV, or a fear-driven myth?

"You can catch it from a hug"

scenarios.relearn: Meals, hugs and handshakes are safe; 'catch it from a hug', mosquitoes and 'keep the cup apart' are myths.

scenarios.hook: Sort: dignity in language, or a slur?
scenarios.relearn: 'Person living with HIV' centres the person; 'the infected one' and 'diseased guy' are slurs.

scenarios.hook: Sort: dignified reaction to a disclosure, or stigma reaction?
scenarios.relearn: Thanks, sameness and support are dignity; backing away, 'don't touch' and telling others are stigma.

scenarios.hook: Sort: anti-stigma action, or stigma in disguise?

items.text: "I'm not judging, but stay away from them"
Sharing where to test, no fuss
Pretending to be kind while gossiping

scenarios.relearn: Facts, calm info and privacy fight stigma; 'not judging but...' and fake kindness hide it.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two stigma lines in this group chat.

scene.text: "Heard who went to the clinic? Spill"
"Anyone can need a test, no big deal"

scenarios.why: Demanding the gossip and 'stay away' are the stigma; the rest protect privacy and tell the truth.
scenarios.relearn: Spot stigma in 'spill the gossip' and 'stay away from him'.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two stigma lines an aunty might say.

scene.text: "Don't let your sister near that family"
"It's a health matter, not a scandal"

scenarios.why: 'Don't let her near' and 'brought shame' are the stigma; the others are fact and respect.
scenarios.relearn: Spot stigma in 'keep away from that family' and 'brought shame'.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two self-stigma thoughts to let go of.

scene.text: "I deserve to be alone for this"
"This is health info, not a verdict"

scenarios.why: 'Ruined and dirty' and 'deserve to be alone' are self-stigma; the rest are self-dignity.
scenarios.relearn: Spot self-stigma in 'I'm dirty' and 'I deserve to be alone'.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two myths about how HIV spreads.

scene.text: "You can get it from sharing a cup"

scenarios.why: Shared cups and mosquitoes are myths; the rest are true. Believing myths fuels stigma.
scenarios.relearn: Spot the myths: HIV isn't spread by shared cups or mosquitoes.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two pity lines hiding as kindness.

scene.text: "Good to see you, same as always"
"So sad, I could never cope like that"
"Tell me how I can have your back"

scenarios.why: 'Poor thing' and 'so sad' look down with pity; the rest stand beside as equals (solidarity).
scenarios.relearn: Spot pity in 'poor thing' and 'so sad'; solidarity treats people as equals.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two lines that break confidentiality.

scene.text: "I'll just tell the warden, for safety"
"It's your news to share, not mine"
"Let me forward your report to the group"
"I won't say a word without your okay"

scenarios.why: Telling the warden and forwarding the report break confidentiality; the rest protect their choice.
scenarios.relearn: Spot the breaches: telling others or forwarding a report without consent.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two stigma lines disguised as 'just being safe'.

scene.text: "I won't share a desk with them"
"Keep their cup separate, just in case"
"Their status is private and fine by me"

scenarios.why: Refusing a desk and separating a cup are stigma dressed as caution; everyday contact is safe.
scenarios.relearn: Spot stigma-as-caution in 'won't share a desk' and 'keep their cup separate'.

scenarios.hook: Cousins are laughing at a viral 'AIDS' meme about a real neighbour.

yourLine.text: "That's a real person's health you're joking about. I'm not into that."
Smile and scroll past

scenarios.relearn: Name it: a real person's health isn't meme material.

scenarios.hook: A friend just told you they tested positive and goes quiet, watching your face.

yourLine.text: "Thanks for trusting me. Nothing changes between us, I'm here."
"Oh... um, okay" and look away

scenarios.relearn: Meet a disclosure with warmth and 'nothing changes between us'.

scenarios.hook: A roommate wants to forward a classmate's leaked test report to the hostel group.
scenarios.setup: Stop it kindly but firmly. Say:

yourLine.text: "No, that's private. Forwarding it would really hurt them, let's delete it."
"Eh, everyone'll find out anyway"

scenarios.relearn: Refuse to forward a private report; protect their confidentiality.

scenarios.hook: A relative says people with HIV shouldn't eat at family functions.
scenarios.setup: Correct it with calm facts. Say:

yourLine.text: "It doesn't spread through food or sitting together. Excluding people just hurts them."
Stay quiet to avoid an argument

scenarios.relearn: Calmly correct the myth: HIV isn't spread by sharing meals.

scenarios.hook: A classmate jokes 'only certain types get those infections' in front of everyone.

yourLine.text: "Anyone can be affected, it's about health, not 'types'. Let's not go there."
Laugh so it's less awkward

scenarios.relearn: Name it: infection is about health, not a 'type' of person.

scenarios.hook: You're spiralling into self-blame after a result, talking to yourself in the mirror.
scenarios.setup: Give yourself the dignity you'd give a friend. Say:

yourLine.text: "This is health info, not a verdict on me. I deserve care, not shame."
"I really messed everything up"

scenarios.relearn: Speak to yourself with dignity: it's health info, not a verdict.

scenarios.hook: A senior pressures you to 'out' who you saw at the ICTC centre.

yourLine.text: "That's not mine to share, and it shouldn't be yours either. Let's drop it."
"Fine, it was..." and tell them

scenarios.relearn: Refuse to out who you saw testing; their privacy isn't yours to share.

scenarios.hook: A teammate's status leaks and the group starts freezing them out. What do you do?

options.text: Sit with them as usual and keep including them
options.consequence: They still belong; your steadiness lets others stop the freeze-out.

options.text: Quietly distance yourself to not 'pick sides'
options.consequence: Silence sides with the freeze-out; standing with them is dignity.

scenarios.debrief: Including someone openly is the move that stops a freeze-out.
scenarios.relearn: Keep including someone openly to stop a freeze-out.

scenarios.hook: You accidentally see a friend's positive test report on their phone. What now?

options.text: Say nothing; let them raise it if they ever want to
options.consequence: Their privacy stays intact and the choice to share stays theirs.

options.text: Warn one friend 'so people can be careful'
options.consequence: That spreads it without consent; contact is safe and it wasn't yours to share.

scenarios.debrief: Seeing something private doesn't make it yours to pass on.
scenarios.relearn: What you see by accident still isn't yours to share.

scenarios.hook: A new student is whispered about as 'the one with HIV'. How do you treat them?

options.text: Walk over, introduce yourself and treat them like any new classmate
options.consequence: They get a normal, warm welcome; the whisper loses its power.

options.text: Keep a polite distance, just in case
options.consequence: There's no everyday risk; distance only feeds the whisper and the hurt.

scenarios.debrief: A normal welcome is the most powerful answer to a stigmatising whisper.
scenarios.relearn: Offer a normal, warm welcome; there's no reason to keep distance.

scenarios.hook: Your partner discloses they're living with HIV. What do you do?

options.text: Thank them, ask questions calmly, learn about U=U together
options.consequence: You meet trust with respect and learn how to care for each other.

options.text: Pull back and assume the worst without asking
options.consequence: That's reacting to fear, not facts; honesty deserves respect, not panic.

scenarios.debrief: A disclosure is trust; meet it with respect and real information.
scenarios.relearn: Meet a partner's disclosure with respect and learn the facts.

scenarios.hook: A meme mocking people with STIs is going round your class group. What do you do?

options.text: Reply once, calmly: 'this mocks real people, let's not'
options.consequence: A calm voice names it and makes others rethink sharing it.

options.text: Forward it to two friends, it's just a joke
options.consequence: Forwarding spreads stigma; a 'joke' at someone's health still harms.

scenarios.debrief: One calm, factual reply can change how a whole chat behaves.
scenarios.relearn: One calm reply can stop a stigmatising 'joke' spreading.

scenarios.hook: You feel a wave of shame after testing and want to hide. What do you choose?

options.text: Treat yourself kindly and reach out to a counsellor
options.consequence: You swap self-stigma for self-care and get support that helps.

options.text: Bottle it up and avoid people until it passes
options.consequence: Isolation feeds shame; it's health info, and you deserve care, not hiding.

scenarios.debrief: Self-dignity means meeting your own result with kindness and support.
scenarios.relearn: Meet your own result with kindness, not hiding; reach for support.

scenarios.hook: A friend asked you to keep their status secret; now a relative pries. What do you do?

options.text: Keep your word: 'that's private, not mine to discuss'
options.consequence: You honour their trust and protect their privacy under pressure.

options.text: Drop a hint so the relative stops pestering
options.consequence: A hint still breaks the confidence; their trust needs you to hold the line.

scenarios.debrief: Confidentiality means holding the line even when someone pries.
scenarios.relearn: Hold a confidence under pressure; their privacy comes first.

scenarios.hook: "If I feel fine, I don't need a test."

myth.un: Feeling fine means I don't need a test.
myth.re: Many STIs cause no symptoms at all; feeling well tells you nothing.
myth.why: Only a test, not how you feel, can tell you your status.

scenarios.relearn: Feeling fine proves nothing; only a test tells you your status.

scenarios.hook: "Asking where to test is embarrassing."

myth.un: Asking where to test is embarrassing.
myth.re: Clinic staff handle these questions every day; it's a normal health request.
myth.why: Walking in informed is self-respect, not something to blush about.

scenarios.relearn: Asking to test is a normal health request, not something to be shy about.

scenarios.hook: "A negative result means I'm covered for life."

myth.un: One negative result covers me for life.
myth.re: Status can change with new exposures; testing fits your situation over time.
myth.why: A result reflects a moment, so testing stays part of ongoing self-care.

scenarios.relearn: A negative result is a snapshot; keep testing as your life changes.

scenarios.hook: "Testing positive ends your life."

myth.un: Testing positive ends your life.
myth.re: Treatment works; people who know their status live full, healthy lives.
myth.why: Knowing early opens the door to care, the opposite of an ending.

scenarios.relearn: A result is a starting point for care, never the end of a life.

scenarios.hook: "Only people with many partners need testing."

myth.un: Only people with many partners need testing.
myth.re: Anyone sexually active can benefit; it takes only one exposure.
myth.why: Testing is about behaviour and care, never a count or a label.

scenarios.relearn: Testing is for anyone active, not a judgement on how many partners.

scenarios.hook: "A clinic will tell my parents or college."

myth.un: A clinic will tell my parents or college.
myth.re: Confidential services keep your visit private; that's part of the care.
myth.why: Privacy is built in so you can seek help without fear.

scenarios.relearn: Confidential testing keeps your visit private; privacy is built in.

scenarios.hook: "A self-test result can't be trusted at all."

myth.un: A self-test result can't be trusted.
myth.re: Used correctly and read after the window period, self-tests are reliable.
myth.why: They're a valid, private way to learn your status at home.

scenarios.relearn: Self-tests are reliable when used right and read after the window period.

scenarios.hook: "Getting tested invites bad luck."

myth.un: Getting tested invites bad luck.
myth.re: A test changes nothing about your body; it only gives you the facts.
myth.why: Knowledge lets you act early, which is the opposite of harm.

scenarios.relearn: A test only reveals facts; it can't cause anything.

scenarios.hook: "I should wait until I have symptoms to test."

myth.un: I should wait for symptoms before testing.
myth.re: Most infections stay silent, so waiting for symptoms misses them.
myth.why: Routine testing, not symptom-watching, is how you stay informed.

scenarios.relearn: Don't wait for symptoms; most infections are silent, so test routinely.

scenarios.hook: "If a partner looks clean, no test is needed."

myth.un: If a partner looks clean, no test is needed.
myth.re: You can't see status; healthy-looking people can carry an STI unknowingly.
myth.why: Only testing, never appearance, tells either of you the facts.

scenarios.relearn: Looks reveal nothing; only a test tells you or a partner your status.

scenarios.hook: "Testing is only an HIV thing."

myth.un: Testing is only about HIV.
myth.re: A check can cover several STIs, many curable, not HIV alone.
myth.why: Knowing your full status lets you act on whatever shows up.

scenarios.relearn: Testing can cover several STIs, many curable, not just HIV.

scenarios.hook: "Knowing my status changes who I am."

myth.un: Knowing my status changes who I am.

scenarios.hook: "If you're HIV positive you have to give up on having a family."

myth.un: HIV positive means giving up on a family.
myth.re: With treatment, people with HIV plan pregnancies and have HIV-negative babies safely.
myth.why: Treatment keeps the virus undetectable, so it isn't passed on.

scenarios.relearn: With treatment, people with HIV can safely plan a family.

scenarios.hook: "Starting HIV treatment means swallowing a fistful of pills forever."

myth.un: HIV treatment means a fistful of pills forever.
myth.re: Most people take a single daily tablet; some use long-acting injections.
myth.why: Modern regimens are simple, and people stick with them easily.

scenarios.relearn: Modern HIV treatment is often one daily pill, not a handful.

scenarios.hook: "Once you have an STI, you'll always carry it."

myth.un: Once you get an STI you carry it for life.
myth.re: Chlamydia, gonorrhoea, syphilis and trichomoniasis are fully cured with the right medicine.
myth.why: The right antibiotics clear these infections completely.

scenarios.relearn: Four common STIs are fully curable with the right medicine.

scenarios.hook: "HIV treatment is too costly for an ordinary family."

myth.un: HIV treatment costs too much for an ordinary family.
myth.re: In India, HIV treatment is provided free at government ART centres.
myth.why: The national programme makes lifelong treatment reachable for everyone.

scenarios.relearn: HIV treatment is free at government ART centres in India.

scenarios.hook: "If you start HIV medicine, you can never stop or skip a day or you'll die."

myth.un: Skip one day of HIV medicine and you'll die.
myth.re: Taking it regularly keeps you well; a missed dose isn't a disaster, just get back on track.
myth.why: Steady treatment, not panic over one dose, is what keeps the virus down.

scenarios.relearn: Take HIV medicine regularly; one missed dose is recoverable.

scenarios.hook: "There's no medicine for HIV, only for the infections it brings."

myth.un: There's no medicine for HIV itself.
myth.re: Antiretroviral therapy treats HIV directly, keeping the immune system strong.
myth.why: ART acts on the virus, so the infections it used to cause rarely happen.

scenarios.relearn: Antiretroviral therapy treats HIV itself and keeps you well.

scenarios.hook: "An undetectable result just means the test missed it."

myth.un: Undetectable just means the test missed the virus.
myth.re: Undetectable means treatment has pushed the virus too low to measure or pass on.
myth.why: It's a real, measured result that proves the treatment is working.

scenarios.relearn: Undetectable is a real result: too low to measure or transmit.

scenarios.hook: "Treating an STI early or late makes no difference."

myth.un: Treating an STI early or late makes no difference.
myth.re: Early treatment clears it before complications; waiting can affect fertility or health.
myth.why: Acting sooner keeps a simple infection from causing harder problems.

scenarios.relearn: Treat an STI early to avoid complications; timing matters.

scenarios.hook: "A positive result means your life is basically over."

myth.un: A positive result means your life is over.
myth.re: A result is information to act on; with treatment you keep studying, working and loving.
myth.why: Treatment turns a result into a managed part of a full life.

scenarios.relearn: A positive result is information to act on, not the end.

scenarios.hook: "You can feel when HIV treatment is working, so tests are pointless."

myth.un: You can just feel when treatment is working.
myth.re: Regular viral-load tests confirm it's working; feelings alone don't tell you.
myth.why: The number, not a hunch, shows the virus is controlled.

scenarios.relearn: Viral-load tests, not feelings, confirm treatment is working.

scenarios.hook: "Only big-city hospitals can treat HIV."

myth.un: Only big-city hospitals can treat HIV.
myth.re: ART centres and link centres run across districts, so care is reachable near home.
myth.why: The programme is spread out so people don't have to travel far for treatment.

scenarios.relearn: ART care runs across districts, reachable close to home.

scenarios.hook: "Herbal or 'detox' cures clear HIV if you believe in them."

myth.un: Herbal or detox cures can clear HIV.
myth.re: Only proven antiretroviral medicine controls HIV; unproven cures waste time and risk health.
myth.why: Time lost on fake cures is time the virus keeps spreading inside the body.

scenarios.relearn: Only proven ART controls HIV; 'detox cures' don't work.

scenarios.hook: "If a partner is on treatment and undetectable, you still can't be intimate safely."

myth.un: You can't be intimate safely with an undetectable partner.
myth.re: U=U: an undetectable partner cannot pass HIV on sexually.
myth.why: Effective treatment keeps the virus too low to be transmitted.

scenarios.relearn: U=U: an undetectable partner can't pass HIV on sexually.

scenarios.hook: "A treated STI always comes back on its own."

myth.un: A treated STI always returns on its own.
myth.re: A cured STI is gone; you only get it again from a new exposure, not by itself.
myth.why: Cure means the infection is cleared, not lying dormant.

scenarios.relearn: A cured STI is gone; reinfection comes from new exposure only.

scenarios.hook: "People with HIV always look sick, so you'd know to avoid treatment failure."

myth.un: People with HIV always look sick.
myth.re: On treatment, people look and feel well; you can't tell health from appearance.
myth.why: Effective treatment keeps people healthy, with no visible signs.

scenarios.relearn: On treatment, people with HIV look and feel well.

scenarios.hook: "Going to an ART centre means everyone will know your status."

myth.un: Going for treatment means everyone will know.
myth.re: ART care is confidential; your status is private health information.
myth.why: Confidentiality is built into the service so people can get care without fear.

scenarios.relearn: ART care is confidential; your status stays private.

scenarios.relearn: U=U doesn't mean gone or stop-the-pills; stay on treatment.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two unhelpful reactions to a friend's positive result.

scene.text: "Treatment works, I'll come with you to the centre"

scenarios.why: 'You did something wrong' and 'keep away' are shaming; support is the right reaction.
scenarios.relearn: Spot shaming reactions; support and dignity are the right ones.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two lines that get treatment wrong.

scene.text: "Stop the pills as soon as you feel fine"
"Ask the doctor about any side effects"

scenarios.why: 'Stop when you feel fine' and 'skipping is fine' are wrong; regular dosing keeps you well.
scenarios.relearn: Spot the 'stop when fine / skipping is fine' lies; dose regularly.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two false barriers to getting treatment.

scene.text: "It costs a fortune no one can afford"
"Everyone will find out if you go"

scenarios.why: 'Costs a fortune' and 'everyone will find out' are false; care is free and confidential.
scenarios.relearn: Spot the cost and exposure myths; care is free and confidential.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two myths about life after a diagnosis.

scene.text: "You'll be too weak to do anything"
"You can never have a partner again"

scenarios.why: 'Too weak' and 'never a partner' are myths; on treatment people live full lives.
scenarios.relearn: Spot the 'too weak / never a partner' myths; full lives are real.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two wrong ideas about STI treatment timing.

scene.text: "Early or late, it makes no difference"
"A cured STI is gone for good"
"It always comes back on its own"

scenarios.why: 'No difference' and 'comes back on its own' are wrong; early treatment cures it for good.
scenarios.relearn: Spot the 'timing doesn't matter / it returns alone' myths.

scenarios.hook: A friend is panicking after a positive HIV test.
scenarios.setup: Steady them with the truth. Say:

yourLine.text: "Treatment works, it's free and private, and I'll go with you. You've got this."
"I don't know, that sounds really bad."

scenarios.relearn: Steady a panicked friend: treatment works, it's free, and you'll go along.

scenarios.hook: A relative pushes a 'guaranteed herbal cure' on you instead of the centre.

yourLine.text: "Thanks, but I'm sticking with the proven treatment from the centre."
"Okay, I'll try yours instead."

scenarios.relearn: Decline unproven cures kindly: stick with proven treatment.

scenarios.hook: Your partner is anxious that being undetectable still isn't safe.

yourLine.text: "Undetectable means untransmittable, the science is settled. We're safe."
"I guess we can never really be sure."

scenarios.relearn: Reassure a partner with U=U: undetectable means untransmittable.

scenarios.hook: You want to ask the counsellor what a positive result actually means for you.

yourLine.text: "What does this result mean, and what are my next steps for treatment?"
Nod and leave without asking anything

scenarios.relearn: Ask the counsellor plainly what a result means and the next steps.

scenarios.hook: A classmate jokes that someone with HIV should 'just give up'.

yourLine.text: "Actually treatment works and people live full lives. That joke isn't true."
Stay quiet and let it slide

scenarios.relearn: Correct 'just give up' calmly: treatment works and full lives are real.

scenarios.hook: You're on treatment and a friend asks why you still take a daily pill if you feel fine.

yourLine.text: "Feeling fine is the pill working, so I keep taking it to stay well."
"Maybe I'll just stop it then."

scenarios.relearn: Explain it simply: feeling fine is the pill working, so keep taking it.

scenarios.hook: You need to tell a recent partner to get tested after your STI result.

yourLine.text: "I tested positive for something treatable, you should test too so you can treat it."
Say nothing and hope they don't find out

scenarios.relearn: Tell a recent partner honestly so they can test and treat it too.

scenarios.hook: A friend is scared the cost of HIV care will ruin their family.

yourLine.text: "HIV treatment is free at government centres, so cost won't be the barrier."
"Yeah, it's probably going to be really expensive."

scenarios.relearn: Reassure on cost: HIV treatment is free at government centres.
